```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`isaves` keeps a history of the objects in your workspace. Each call to `save_incremental()` writes only the objects that changed since the last save, and records a snapshot of the whole workspace. Later, `load_incremental()` can bring back everything, a few objects, an old version of an object or the workspace exactly as it was in a past save.

This vignette walks through a small analysis to show the main functions.

## Where the store lives

Saves go to a *store*: a table with every version of every object (`ws_table.ref`) and a folder with one file per distinct content (`rds/`). By default, the store is placed at the root of the project, the nearest folder going up from the working directory that already has a store, an RStudio project or a git repository. `ws_root()` shows the folder in use.

The option `isaves.root` fixes that folder. This vignette uses it to work in a temporary folder:

```{r setup}
library(isaves)
options(isaves.root = file.path(tempdir(), "isaves-vignette"))
```

## Saving the workspace

We start with some data and save it, with an annotation that describes the save:

```{r}
cars_data <- mtcars
cars_data$am <- factor(cars_data$am, labels = c("automatic", "manual"))
notes <- "Data from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine"

save_incremental(annotation = "raw data")
```

The analysis goes on: a variable is added to the data and a model is fitted. Before saving, `ws_status()` compares the workspace with the store, without writing anything:

```{r}
cars_data$kpl <- cars_data$mpg * 0.425
coefs <- coef(lm(mpg ~ wt + am, data = cars_data))

ws_status()
```

Only the new and modified objects are written. `notes` has not changed, so it is not stored again:

```{r}
save_incremental(annotation = "first model")
```

Saving when nothing has changed writes nothing and records no new snapshot:

```{r}
save_incremental()
```

Objects are stored by content, so an exact copy gets its own row in the table but shares the file of the original. Here we save a copy and then remove it from the workspace:

```{r}
backup <- cars_data
save_incremental(annotation = "with backup")

rm(backup)
save_incremental(annotation = "without backup")

length(list.files(file.path(ws_root(), "rds")))
```

The last save wrote no object, but it still recorded a snapshot, because the workspace changed. There are five object versions in the table, but only four files.

## The reference table and the snapshots

`ws_ref_table()` returns one row per stored version of each object. The help page of `ws_ref_table()` describes all the columns:

```{r}
ws_ref_table()[c("object", "class", "size", "save_id", "annotation")]
```

Like most functions in the package, it takes a `subset`, a logical expression that uses the columns of the table:

```{r}
ws_ref_table(object == "cars_data")[c("object", "date", "save_id")]
```

`ws_snapshots()` lists the saves, the objects present in the workspace at each one and how many of their versions are no longer stored:

```{r}
ws_snapshots()[c("save_id", "annotation", "n_objects", "n_missing")]
```

## Loading

In a new R session you would just call `load_incremental()`, which loads into the calling environment. Here, new environments play the role of a fresh workspace, passed with `envir`.

By default, the latest version of every object ever saved is loaded, including objects that were later removed from the workspace. A message tells which ones:

```{r}
session <- new.env()
load_incremental(envir = session)
ls(session)
```

`snapshot = "latest"` restores the workspace as it was in the last save instead:

```{r}
session <- new.env()
load_incremental(snapshot = "latest", envir = session)
ls(session)
```

### Selected objects and old versions

`subset` selects what to load. When it matches several versions of an object, the latest one is loaded:

```{r}
selected <- new.env()
load_incremental(object == "coefs", envir = selected)
ls(selected)
```

The columns of the table can be used to pick an older version, for example the one created in the first save:

```{r}
load_incremental(object == "cars_data" & save_id == 1, envir = selected)
names(selected$cars_data)
```

Loading never replaces an object that has different content. The stored version gets the date of its save appended to the name:

```{r}
load_incremental(object == "cars_data", envir = selected)
ls(selected)
```

With `overwrite = TRUE`, the object is replaced. `load_incremental()` invisibly returns what it did with each object:

```{r}
result <- load_incremental(object == "cars_data", overwrite = TRUE, envir = selected)
result
```

### Restoring a snapshot

`snapshot` takes the `save_id` or the annotation of a save, and restores the workspace as it was then:

```{r}
raw <- new.env()
load_incremental(snapshot = "raw data", envir = raw)
ls(raw)
names(raw$cars_data)
```

### Lazy loading

With `lazyload = TRUE`, objects are read from disk only when they are first used. Unused lazy-loaded objects are not read by `ws_status()` or `save_incremental()` either, so a large workspace can be restored, checked and saved again quickly:

```{r}
lazy <- new.env()
load_incremental(snapshot = "latest", lazyload = TRUE, envir = lazy)
ws_status(envir = lazy)[c("object", "status")]
lazy$coefs
```

## Maintaining the store

### Annotations

`annotate_ws()` changes the annotation of the selected rows. Without `write = TRUE`, it only shows the result:

```{r}
annotate_ws(object == "backup", "copy, not needed", write = TRUE)[c("object", "annotation")]
```

### Removing versions

`purge_ws_table()` removes the selected versions, and `prune_ws()` keeps only the most recent versions of each object. Both are dry runs unless `remove = TRUE`:

```{r}
purge_ws_table(annotation == "copy, not needed")[c("object", "save_id")]
purge_ws_table(annotation == "copy, not needed", remove = TRUE)[c("object", "save_id")]
```

A file is deleted only when no remaining version uses it. The copy shared its file with `cars_data`, so that file is kept.

```{r}
prune_ws(keep = 1)[c("object", "save_id")]
prune_ws(keep = 1, remove = TRUE)
ws_ref_table()[c("object", "save_id", "annotation")]
```

Removing versions leaves the snapshots that used them incomplete, as the `n_missing` column shows:

```{r}
ws_snapshots()[c("save_id", "annotation", "n_objects", "n_missing")]
```

### Checking the store

`verify_ws()` checks that the table and the files agree. With `deep = TRUE`, every file is also read and its content checked against its hash. Here, it reports the incomplete snapshots left by the pruning:

```{r}
check <- verify_ws(deep = TRUE)
check$incomplete_snapshots
```

## Files and options

These are the files of the store. `ws_table.ref.bak` is the table before its last change, and can replace the table if it gets damaged:

```{r}
list.files(ws_root(), recursive = TRUE)
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `isaves.format` | `"qs2"` | Format of new files: `"qs2"` (fast) or `"rds"` (needs no package to be read) |
| `isaves.nthreads` | up to 8 | Threads used for files larger than 1 MB |
| `isaves.root` | not set | Fixed root folder of the store |
| `isaves.lock.timeout` | `60000` | Milliseconds to wait while another R session updates the store |

Several R sessions can save to the same store at the same time: updates of the table are locked.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(ws_root(), recursive = TRUE)
options(isaves.root = NULL)
```
